Borrowing to invest: match the monthly household cash before comparing the result

Compare an invented interest-only investment loan with investing the same household cash without debt, then separate gross investment assets, interest costs and net equity.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare investing with and without an interest-only loan using matched household cash

Interactive planning lab

Monthly household cash required in each case$391.67
Borrowing case: investment less loan at the end$46,881.05
Borrowing minus no-borrowing ending net position-$13,577.86

Two invented scenarios start with zero own-money investment equity. One borrows the selected principal and invests it immediately; the other borrows nothing. Both receive the same monthly household cash: the loan’s monthly interest plus the selected extra investing cash. The borrowing case pays interest from that budget and invests the remainder; the no-loan case invests the whole budget. All deposits arrive at month-end after growth. Loan principal stays unchanged until repayment at the final date; interest is fully paid monthly and never capitalized. Both investments receive the same constant effective annual total-return assumption, converted to monthly factors. All distributions are reinvested. There are no fees, taxes, interest deductions, collateral calls, forced sales, borrowing limits or changes in rates. Availability of the derived monthly cash and the loan is assumed, not assessed. Negative investment-minus-debt values remain liabilities requiring another repayment source. This narrow matched-cash calculation cannot determine suitability or reproduce an actual lending contract.

The central idea

A larger investment balance funded by a loan is accompanied by debt. Compare net positions using the same household cash commitment, and keep repayment risk separate from an assumed return.

01

Match the household contribution before comparing account balances

Borrowing can place a large amount in an investment account immediately. A comparison with a smaller account funded from monthly saving can then look persuasive simply because the opening gross balances are different. The debt and the ongoing cash commitment need to be included before interpreting that comparison.

This illustration compares two invented cases starting with zero own-money investment equity. The first borrows CAD 50,000 and invests it immediately. Its investment asset and loan liability initially offset each other. The second has neither that investment asset nor a loan.

Both cases then use the same monthly household cash. This is the central control on the comparison: money spent servicing debt in one case is available for investing in the other. Giving the borrower an extra monthly payment source while withholding it from the comparison would change the resources supplied by the household.

02

Split the common cash budget between interest and new investing

The assumed loan rate is 7% simple annual interest, paid in twelve equal monthly amounts on unchanged principal. CAD 50,000 therefore incurs approximately CAD 291.67 of monthly interest. The selected extra investing cash after that payment is CAD 100.

The derived household cash commitment is CAD 291.67 + CAD 100 = approximately CAD 391.67 per month, with full precision retained in the calculation. The borrowing case pays its interest and invests the remaining CAD 100. The no-loan case invests the entire common amount.

Across ten years, each case uses CAD 47,000 of new household cash. The borrower allocates CAD 35,000 to interest and CAD 12,000 to new investment. The no-loan case invests all CAD 47,000. The stacked bars show these equal totals with different allocations.

The budget is derived from the selected loan and extra investing amount. The tool assumes the household can provide it; it does not assess affordability. Raising the loan rate raises the common cash requirement rather than discovering a new source of household income.

03

Subtract the loan before reading the ending investment position

Both investments receive a hypothetical 5% effective annual total return, converted to equal monthly compound factors. Every monthly contribution arrives after that month’s growth, and all investment distributions remain reinvested. There are no investment fees or taxes.

After ten years, the borrowing case holds investment assets of approximately CAD 96,881.05. The original CAD 50,000 principal is still owed. Repaying it leaves a net investment position of approximately CAD 46,881.05.

The no-loan case accumulates about CAD 60,458.90 and has no investment loan to repay. Under these assumptions, borrowing finishes approximately CAD 13,577.86 behind the matched-cash comparison.

The line chart shows investment value less loan for the borrowing case, rather than presenting its larger gross account as additional owned wealth. Its final net amount also is not investment profit relative to household cash supplied. Contributions, investment growth and debt repayment answer different parts of the reconciliation.

04

Reconcile the final repayment without deducting interest twice

The waterfall begins with CAD 50,000 invested from the loan, adds CAD 12,000 of later household money actually invested and approximately CAD 34,881.05 of investment growth, then subtracts the CAD 50,000 principal repaid at the end.

The resulting CAD 46,881.05 matches the net-position line. Interest does not appear as another deduction from this bridge because it was already paid from the household cash budget and reduced the amount contributed to the investment. Deducting CAD 35,000 again here would count the same interest outflow twice.

Interest still matters economically. Its cost is visible in the budget allocation and in the no-loan case’s ability to invest more each month. A separate lifetime profit ledger could subtract household cash from final resources, but it must use a clearly stated definition and consistent timing.

No loan interest is added to principal in this illustration. Capitalizing unpaid interest, making principal instalments or using investment withdrawals to service debt would create different paths and require different cash-flow assumptions.

05

Read the rate matrix as a conditional comparison

The matrix changes annual loan interest and the effective annual investment return. Every cell supplies the same household cash to its paired cases, using that row’s monthly interest plus the selected extra investing amount. The common budget changes between rows.

A useful arithmetic check is the case where the monthly investment growth factor equals the loan’s monthly interest rate. With no fees or taxes, the paired endpoints then coincide. A 7% simple annual interest charge paid monthly corresponds to about 7.23% effective annual growth when expressed on a monthly compound basis.

This equivalence is a mathematical threshold under fixed assumptions, not a forecast, available investment yield or suitability test. The comparison uses a constant return rather than an uncertain sequence of market movements.

Negative investment-minus-debt values remain negative. If a sale does not cover principal, another repayment source would be required. Extending the horizon does not guarantee recovery or remove the obligation to pay the loan.

06

Bring the contract and uncertain household capacity back into the decision

The AMF’s borrowing-to-invest guidance emphasizes that losses can occur while loan repayment and interest remain due. It also describes the possibility of repayment demands and the need to consider changes in personal circumstances.

This model assumes interest can be paid from outside household cash throughout and principal is not demanded until the selected final date. It supplies no collateral-call protection, interest deduction, borrowing approval or guarantee that a lender will preserve the arrangement after a market decline.

For an actual decision, assess repayment capacity independently of hoped-for investment gains, and inspect the terms governing interest, collateral, repayment and fees. Evaluate investment risk and suitability separately. The charts make the accounting comparison inspectable; a favorable cell cannot establish that borrowing is appropriate for the household or that the assumed return will occur.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical illustrations use constant investment returns, monthly interest-only loan payments and equal household cash in both cases. They assess neither borrowing eligibility nor strategy suitability and include no tax deduction or collateral-call protection. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
